Key Strengths Financial-services specific workflows: Synthflow explicitly supports use cases such as account support, loan updates, fraud checks, and other finance-related customer conversations. Strong compliance baseline: Synthflow lists SOC 2, GDPR, HIPAA, ISO 27001, and PCI DSS v4.0.1 support. Data-handling controls: Teams can control whether recordings and transcripts are stored and can configure data-protection settings at the agent level. Structured workflows for sensitive use cases: Its Flow Designer is designed for multi-step, compliance-heavy scenarios where teams want predictable paths rather than letting the agent improvise freely. Human escalation and monitoring: Synthflow supports live transfers with context, call logs, analytics, and custom evaluations that can check whether required compliance steps were followed. Limitations No-code does not remove the need for governance: Banking teams still need to define verification rules, permissions, escalation points, and which actions the agent is allowed to complete. PII redaction is not guaranteed to catch everything: Synthflow itself notes that voice data is unstructured and automated PII redaction may not always be 100% accurate. Some enterprise controls sit on higher plans: SSO and additional enterprise security capabilities are available through the Enterprise offering. It is still the conversation layer: Core banking systems, fraud engines, payment processing, and identity systems still need to remain in approved backend infrastructure. Pricing Synthflow uses pay-as-you-go pricing for self-serve usage, while larger banking and fintech deployments move to Enterprise pricing based on call volume, concurrency, telephony, integrations, and security requirements. ElevenLabs ElevenLabs is a good fit for banks and fintech teams that want AI voice agents to sound natural while still meeting stricter financial-services requirements. Its ElevenAgents platform has a dedicated financial-services offering covering account inquiries, collections, KYC-related workflows, transaction disputes, payment reminders, and customer support, with enterprise controls around compliance, data retention, and escalation. Key Strengths Built for financial-services workflows: ElevenLabs explicitly supports use cases like balance checks, transaction disputes, payment reminders, collections, loan workflows, and KYC-related conversations. Strong compliance posture: ElevenLabs lists PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, GDPR, and regional data residency options for financial-services deployments. Zero-retention options: Teams can use zero-retention mode to reduce how much sensitive conversation data is stored, which is useful for stricter financial environments. Guardrails and controlled workflows: Agents can be configured with rules around what they can discuss, which actions they can take, and when they need to escalate rather than improvise. Core-system integration: Agents can connect to banking APIs, CRMs, payment systems, and other backend tools so they can retrieve approved data or complete controlled actions during the call. Limitations It is still the AI conversation layer: ElevenLabs does not replace core banking, fraud, identity, or payments infrastructure. Those systems still need to control sensitive actions. Authentication needs to be designed carefully: High-risk actions such as payments or transfers still need step-up authentication and clear escalation rules. Telephony may remain separate: Many deployments still connect through existing telephony or contact-center infrastructure rather than replacing it entirely. Stronger compliance setups can add complexity: Zero retention, regional data residency, custom integrations, and enterprise controls require more deliberate configuration than a basic voice-agent deployment. Pricing Keeping the pricing you provided for this comparison, ElevenLabs starts at $6 per month. Higher plans include usage and concurrency, while telephony and LLM usage are charged separately. Twilio Twilio is a strong fit for banks and fintech companies that want to build highly customized voice workflows on top of established communications infrastructure. It already has a dedicated financial-services offering, plus tools for authentication, programmable voice, contact-center workflows, and AI conversations, which makes it flexible for everything from customer support to payment-related calls. Key Strengths Built for financial-services use cases: Twilio supports banking, payments, credit unions, insurance, and other financial workflows across voice and messaging. PCI-compliant voice workflows: Twilio provides PCI Mode for Programmable Voice, including secure handling and redaction of payment-card data during supported workflows. Authentication options: Twilio also offers identity and verification products, which can be useful when voice workflows need stronger authentication before sensitive actions are allowed. Strong developer control: Teams can build custom logic around calls, routing, payments, AI agents, and backend integrations instead of working inside a fixed workflow. Flexible AI voice stack: Conversation Relay can connect AI agents to Twilio Voice while Twilio handles speech recognition and voice synthesis. Limitations PCI configuration needs care: PCI Mode has to be enabled correctly, and not every transcription or AI provider used with Conversation Relay is automatically PCI compliant. More engineering-heavy: Twilio gives teams plenty of flexibility, but banking workflows usually require developers to configure authentication, payment handling, routing, and integrations. AI functionality is spread across multiple products: Voice, Conversation Relay, Flex, Verify, and other products can all be part of the final setup, which can make the architecture more complex. Some analytics tools have PCI restrictions: Twilio notes that Conversation Intelligence Classic should not be enabled for PCI-sensitive Conversation Relay workflows. Pricing Keeping the pricing approach we have been using, Twilio is pay as you go. Voice, phone numbers, AI services, authentication, and other components are generally charged separately depending on the setup. LiveKit LiveKit is a good fit for fintech and banking teams with strong engineering resources that want to build a more customized voice AI stack. It gives developers control over the agent logic, telephony, external APIs, deployment, and data flow, which can be useful when financial workflows need tighter technical guardrails than a typical out-of-the-box voice agent. Key Strengths Strong deployment control: Teams can use LiveKit Cloud or self-host parts of the stack, which gives larger financial institutions more flexibility over infrastructure and data handling. Enterprise security foundation: LiveKit lists SOC 2 Type II and GDPR support, along with end-to-end encryption for realtime media and data. Data residency options: Region pinning can help teams control where traffic is processed when regional or regulatory requirements matter. Flexible backend integrations: Agents can call external APIs and custom tools, which makes it possible to connect approved verification, account, CRM, or financial systems. Context-aware human escalation: LiveKit supports warm transfers where the AI agent can pass a summary or collected information to a human before the handoff. Limitations PCI DSS should be verified for the exact architecture: LiveKit publishes strong security capabilities, but its public documentation does not clearly establish PCI DSS coverage for every voice-agent deployment. Financial teams handling card data should validate this before production. More engineering-heavy: Authentication, permissions, guardrails, API access, and escalation logic generally need to be designed by the team rather than configured through a finished banking workflow. Telephony can add another layer: Depending on the deployment, teams may need SIP trunks or external telephony infrastructure for inbound and outbound calling. Not purpose-built for banking: LiveKit provides the infrastructure for building secure voice applications, but banking-specific workflows, fraud controls, KYC logic, and financial compliance processes need to come from your own systems. Pricing Keeping the pricing we are using for this comparison, LiveKit starts at $50 per month, with additional usage-based costs depending on agents, telephony, inference, and infrastructure. Choosing the Right AI Voice Agent for Banking and Fintech The right platform depends on how sensitive the workflow is, how much control your team needs, and whether you want the AI layer tightly connected to your telephony or built more modularly around existing systems. For teams that want AI voice + telephony in one stack Plivo is a strong option if you want voice AI, telephony, routing, and enterprise controls closer together. That can be useful for financial teams that want fewer vendors involved in the call path and a simpler setup for things like payment reminders, account servicing, collections, and support. For developer-led fintech teams that want maximum flexibility Vapi makes more sense when your engineering team wants to control models, telephony, verification flows, APIs, and backend integrations. It is flexible, but that flexibility comes with more implementation work. For teams that want faster deployment with built-in QA Retell AI is a good middle ground if you want to automate banking conversations quickly while still getting structured monitoring, guardrails, and human escalation. For high-volume financial call automation Bland AI is a strong fit when the goal is to automate a large number of customer conversations around collections, fraud alerts, payment support, or servicing. Its enterprise deployment options also make it more relevant for larger financial institutions. For ops teams that want a no-code approach Synthflow AI works well when operations teams need to build and manage structured financial workflows without relying on developers for every change. It is especially useful when you want more predictable call flows rather than highly open-ended conversations. For teams where voice quality matters most ElevenLabs stands out when the customer experience depends heavily on how natural the agent sounds. It also brings stronger financial-services controls than a basic voice-generation platform, which makes it more viable for real banking and fintech use cases. For enterprises that want deep customization Twilio is a strong option if you already use its communications stack or need to build highly customized authentication, payment, routing, and support workflows. It gives you a lot of control, but the final architecture can involve several Twilio products. For engineering teams building a custom financial voice stack LiveKit is best suited to teams that want infrastructure-level control over the real-time voice experience, deployment, APIs, and data flow. It can work well for custom fintech products, but more of the compliance and banking-specific logic needs to be built around it. The main decision is whether you want a more integrated platform or a more modular stack. For teams starting fresh and looking to keep telephony, AI voice, routing, and enterprise controls under fewer vendors, Plivo is one of the more balanced options to put on the shortlist. Final Thoughts The best AI voice agent for banking and fintech is not just the one that sounds the most natural. It needs to fit your security model, handle sensitive workflows carefully, integrate with the right backend systems, and know when a human should take over. Vapi and LiveKit are better suited to engineering-heavy teams, Retell and Bland are strong for structured automation, Synthflow is easier for ops-led teams, and ElevenLabs stands out for voice quality. But if you want to keep AI voice, telephony, routing, and enterprise controls closer together, Plivo is one of the more practical options to evaluate, especially for teams trying to reduce the number of vendors in a sensitive call flow. Want to simplify your financial voice AI stack? If you are evaluating AI voice agents for banking or fintech and want fewer moving parts across telephony, routing, AI, and enterprise controls, Plivo is worth putting on your shortlist. title: New CEA Property Agent Requirements From 2027: What You Need to Know
summary: Singapore property agents must complete 3 transactions in 3 years or pass an exam starting 1 January 2027. See what this means for agents and customers.
body_text: Last Updated on August 3, 2026 by Yolly Del Prado Whether you’re buying a new home , selling your property , or renting a space , you want the agent guiding you to understand how the market works today, not rely on how it worked several years ago. So to help property agents keep their practical knowledge current, the Council for Estate Agencies (CEA) is introducing a new requirement. From 1 January 2027, agents will need to complete at least three qualifying property transactions within their three-year registration period or pass a Refresher Examination before they can renew their registration. For buyers and sellers, this adds a useful minimum standard. But does it mean you can simply look at an agent’s transaction count and know they’re right for you? Not quite. Here’s what is changing, how the requirement will work and what you should still consider when choosing someone to guide you through your next property move. New Property Agent Requirements at a Glance Here’s a quick overview of the key CEA property agent requirement changes from 2027: What is changing? Details Effective date 1 January 2027 Registration period Three years instead of one Currency Requirement At least three qualifying transactions during the applicable period or passing the Refresher Examination First cycle for existing agents 1 January 2027 to 31 December 2029 Annual CPD Continues separately at 16 hours a year Existing agents do not need to meet the Currency Requirement before entering the first cycle. They will work towards it during the three-year period. Moving from annual to three-year registrations should also mean less renewal paperwork for agents and property agencies. How Does the Currency Requirement Work? Agents can meet the requirement in one of two ways: 1. Complete at Least Three Qualifying Transactions An agent registered throughout the full three-year cycle must complete at least three qualifying transactions during that period. This doesn’t mean they need to complete one transaction every year. They simply need to reach the required total by the end of their registration cycle. Looking at activity over three years also gives agents some breathing room. Property transactions don’t all move at the same pace, and some can take much longer than others. According to CEA, this timeframe gives agents flexibility without putting them under unnecessary pressure to transact. 2. Pass the Refresher Examination If an agent doesn’t complete the required number of transactions, there’s still another route available. They can meet the Currency Requirement by passing the Refresher Examination. CEA has said that the examination will focus on the practice-related knowledge agents need for estate agency work. Agents who fall below the transaction threshold will also be guaranteed a place to sit for it. Details such as the format, fee, syllabus, passing mark and retake arrangements haven’t been announced yet. CEA expects to share more information in the first half of 2029, so it’s best to wait for the official details rather than rely on speculation. What Counts as a Qualifying Property Transaction? Qualifying transactions include: HDB resale and rental transactions Private residential sale, resale and rental transactions Commercial sale, resale and rental transactions Industrial sale, resale and rental transactions Foreign property sale transactions En bloc transactions For most residential transactions, CEA will recognise one agent on each represented side of a completed deal. Commercial, industrial and en bloc transactions may be handled differently because they can involve larger teams and much longer timelines. In these cases, CEA may recognise more than one agent on a represented side if the property agency submits supporting documents. Each case will be assessed individually. What About New Property Agents? New agents will have some time to find their footing. Anyone entering the industry from 1 January 2027 will receive a registration beginning on their date of entry and ending on 31 December of the third year. For example, an agent who joins on 15 February 2028 will be registered until 31 December 2030. They won’t need to meet the Currency Requirement during their first calendar year. From the second year onwards, it will apply on a pro-rated basis. Using CEA’s current example, a new agent must complete at least two qualifying transactions during the remaining two years or pass the Refresher Examination. Can Agents Ask for an Exception? CEA has said that agents facing extenuating circumstances can ask for their case to be reviewed. Serious illness and unusually complex transactions are among the examples given. This is helpful because transaction frequency isn’t always entirely within an agent’s control. An en bloc, industrial or high-value commercial deal can involve months of work without being completed within the expected period. However, exceptions won’t be granted automatically. Agents will need to provide supporting information, and CEA will assess each case individually. What Happens If an Agent Does Not Meet Either Requirement? Completing fewer than three transactions doesn’t automatically mean an agent has to leave the industry. They can still remain eligible for renewal by passing the Refresher Examination. If an agent completes neither the required transactions nor the examination, they won’t be able to renew their registration. Should they decide to return later, they’ll need to complete the Real Estate Salesperson course and pass the Real Estate Salesperson Examination again. Why is CEA Introducing This Requirement? Property rules don’t stand still. Financing considerations, eligibility conditions and administrative processes can all change, sometimes with a direct impact on a household’s plans. If an agent has spent several years away from active property work, there may be questions about whether their knowledge still reflects the current market. That matters when you’re making decisions such as whether you’re eligible to buy a particular home, how to finance it or how to coordinate your sale and purchase without leaving yourself in a difficult position. Consumers appear to feel the same way. In CEA’s 2024 Public Perception Survey, 74% of consumers expected property agents to complete at least one transaction a year so that agents would remain familiar with the latest rules and guidelines. However, as of 1 January 2026, about 40% of the 32,967 agents who had been registered since 2023 completed fewer than three recorded residential transactions between 2023 and 2025. The median number of residential transactions completed per agent annually during that period was two. But these figures only cover recorded residential transactions, so they don’t tell us everything an agent may have been working on. Still, they help explain why CEA is introducing the Currency Requirement. Does This Replace an Agent’s Annual Training? No. Agents must still complete at least 16 hours of Continuing Professional Development training every year: At least 12 hours of Structured Learning At least four hours of Self-directed Learning CPD helps agents build and refresh their professional knowledge, while the Currency Requirement focuses on recent transaction activity or practice-related knowledge demonstrated through the examination. Agents must meet both requirements separately. What Should Buyers and Sellers Take Away From This? The requirement provides a useful starting point, but it does not tell you whether an agent’s experience is relevant to your property. For example, an agent who regularly handles rentals may have limited recent experience selling a landed home, while commercial transactions may be fewer because each one takes longer. So, before deciding which agent to work with , have a proper conversation. You might ask: Have you recently handled a property or situation similar to mine? Were you representing the buyer, seller, landlord or tenant? Are there any current rules that could affect my plans? What timeline should I prepare for? Who will handle my viewings, negotiations and documents? What does your fee cover? You should also confirm the agent’s registration , property agency and contact details through the CEA Public Register. Most importantly, pay attention to how the agent speaks with you. Do they listen before offering an answer? Can they explain the process without making it confusing? Are they open about what needs to be checked? Those qualities won’t appear in a transaction number, but they can make a real difference to your experience. Choosing an Agent is Still About More Than One Number Moving forward, an agent’s recent transaction experience may be worth looking at alongside their CEA registration. Regular activity gives agents more opportunities to work with current requirements, timelines and buyer and seller concerns. Based on insights, an average property agent in Singapore closes approximately three to four deals a year, while an Ohmyhome agent closes approximately 40 to 60. This is supported by our agents’ experience and the technology and operational systems Ohmyhome has built over the past 10 years. Still, numbers are only part of the picture. Look for an agent who understands your property, listens to your needs and can guide you through your next move. Whatever your next property move looks like, our Ohmyhome agents are here to guide you through it. WhatsApp us today to get started! Frequently Asked Questions Does Meeting the Currency Requirement Guarantee an Agent’s Registration Renewal? No. The Currency Requirement will be one condition for renewal. Agents must still satisfy other applicable requirements, including completing their annual Continuing Professional Development training. Consumers should continue checking the CEA Public Register to confirm that an agent’s registration is currently valid. Should I Be Concerned If an Agent Qualified by Passing the Examination Instead? Not automatically. There may be circumstances that prevented an agent from completing three transactions within the registration period. For example, they may have faced a serious illness or spent considerable time working on a complex commercial, industrial or en bloc transaction that took longer to complete. Passing the Refresher Examination provides another way for the agent to demonstrate that their practice-related knowledge remains current. However, you should still ask about their recent experience with your property type and situation before deciding whether they are right for you. What Happens to My Transaction If My Agent Cannot Renew Their Registration? A property agent cannot continue conducting estate agency work without a valid registration. If your agent’s registration lapses while your transaction is ongoing, contact their property agency to confirm who will take over your case and how the handover will be managed.

title: Testing Agent Memory: QA on Agents with State
summary: Blog post from Hyperspell
body_text: Traditional unit tests follow a clean pattern. Input goes in, function runs, expected output comes out. If the test passes, the code works. Memory systems break this pattern. The output of any query depends on everything the system has ingested over days or weeks. The question is no longer "does this function return the right value?" It becomes "given everything my agent has seen so far, does it retrieve the right context for this query?" This is not a theoretical problem. A comprehensive survey of agent memory research found that existing works "differ substantially in their motivations, implementations, and evaluation protocols." There is no standard testing methodology for memory systems. The field is fragmented, and most teams are building their QA practices from scratch. At Hyperspell, we process memory queries across 50+ workspace integrations. That operational experience has taught us patterns for testing stateful systems: what to test, how to test it, and how to make tests reproducible. Why traditional testing fails for memory Traditional software testing assumes determinism. Same input, same output. Memory systems violate this assumption in four ways. State accumulation. The output of a memory query depends on what has been ingested previously. Two identical queries can return different results if one runs against a fresh memory store and the other against one with three weeks of indexed data. Time dependency. Results change as new data syncs. A query that returns correct results today may return different results tomorrow after a new batch of Slack messages is indexed. Non-determinism. Retrieval ranking and LLM processing add variance. Research on testing agentic systems notes that the same test can pass one run and fail the next simply because the agent chose a different reasoning path. This applies directly to memory systems where retrieval ranking is similarity-based. Combinatorial scale. You cannot exhaustively test all possible memory states. As data volume grows, the space of possible retrieval results grows with it. Brute-force testing is not an option. Dimension Traditional tests Memory tests State Stateless or reset between runs Accumulated over time, affects every result Determinism Same input, same output Same input, different output depending on context Time sensitivity Results are stable Results change as data syncs Failure diagnosis Clear stack trace Requires inspecting retrieval context and ranking Traditional tests ask "does this function work?" Memory tests ask "given everything the system knows right now, does it find the right information?" That shift from stateless to stateful is what makes memory QA fundamentally different. What to test in a memory system Memory testing breaks down into five distinct problems, each with its own failure modes. Ingestion correctness Does data get stored as expected? When you ingest a document that mentions a specific person, project, or date, does that information appear in query results with the correct metadata? A basic ingestion test: add a known document using the memories API, query for a specific entity mentioned in that document, and verify the entity appears in results. If it does not, your ingestion pipeline has a gap. from hyperspell import Hyperspell client = Hyperspell(api_key="API_KEY", user_id="test-user") # Ingest a known document status = client.memories.add( text="Project Alpha launched on March 15. Lead engineer: Sarah Chen.", metadata={"collection": "test-fixtures"} ) # Query for the entity response = client.memories.search( query="Who is the lead engineer on Project Alpha?", sources=["vault"], options={"filter": {"collection": "test-fixtures"}} ) # Verify the expected entity appears in results assert any("Sarah Chen" in doc.text for doc in response.documents) Retrieval accuracy Given a query, are the right memories retrieved? Are they ranked appropriately? The standard metrics are Precision@k, Recall@k, and NDCG@k. Precision measures how many of the top k retrieved items are relevant. Recall measures how many of all relevant items appear in the top k. NDCG rewards relevant items appearing higher in the ranking. The MemoryAgentBench benchmark identified four core competencies to evaluate: accurate retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding, and conflict resolution. Its finding was sobering: on multi-hop conflict resolution, every tested method scored in the single digits, 7% at best. Retrieval accuracy alone does not tell you whether your memory system works. Permission enforcement In multi-tenant memory systems, one user's data must never appear in another user's retrieval results. Permission tests are binary: either the filter works or it leaks data. Test by creating two isolated user contexts, ingesting different data for each, and verifying that cross-user queries return nothing. This is one area where you want 100% pass rates, not statistical confidence intervals. Sync correctness When a source document changes, does the memory reflect the change? When a document is deleted, does it disappear from retrieval results? Test pattern: update a source document, wait for sync, then verify the memory reflects the new version and the old version is no longer retrievable. You can monitor sync progress using the indexing progress endpoint. Freshness guarantees If a user connects a new data source, how long until that data is queryable? Freshness tests measure the time between ingestion and availability. Set a threshold, ingest test data, poll for availability, and fail the test if the threshold is exceeded. Test categories The five dimensions above tell you what to test. The categories below tell you how. Unit tests Test individual components in isolation: the chunker, the embedder, the metadata parser. This is the one category where traditional testing patterns apply directly. Verify that a specific document format parses into the expected number of chunks with the correct metadata attached. Unit tests should be fast, deterministic, and run on every commit. Integration tests Test the full pipeline end-to-end. Ingest a document, query for it, and verify retrieval. These are slower but catch issues that unit tests miss, like mismatches between how the chunker splits text and how the embedder represents it. Because memory systems are non-deterministic, run multiple trials per scenario. One assessment framework for agentic AI recommends running each scenario several times independently and averaging the results. A test that fails one out of three runs is a signal worth investigating, even if it passes the majority. Retrieval evaluation This is where memory testing diverges most from traditional QA. You need a ground truth dataset: a set of queries paired with the documents that should be retrieved for each. Evidently AI's RAG evaluation guide describes three approaches to building ground truth: Pre-labeled documents. Manually map test queries to correct source documents. Labor-intensive but precise. Post-retrieval assessment. Run queries against your system, then have reviewers label the actual results as relevant or not. Captures real-world retrieval behavior. LLM-based scoring. Use an LLM to judge whether retrieved chunks are relevant to queries. Strong LLM judges can approach human-level agreement on chunk relevance. The most scalable approach is synthetic generation: start from your knowledge base, use an LLM to generate realistic questions answerable from specific chunks, and use those question-document pairs as your test suite. Hyperspell's Evaluation API provides a built-in feedback loop for this. Every query returns a query_id, and each retrieved highlight includes a highlight_id. You can score both programmatically: # Score a query result (scale: -1 to 1) client.evaluate.score_query( query_id=response.query_id, score=1.0 ) # Score an individual highlight with a comment client.evaluate.score_highlight( highlight_id=highlight.highlight_id, score=-1.0, comment="Retrieved outdated project status" ) These scores feed back into retrieval ranking over time, creating a continuous improvement loop without manual re-tuning. Regression tests Golden queries with expected results, run on every deploy. These catch the specific case where a system update degrades retrieval quality for previously working queries. Version your test datasets alongside your code. What counted as a correct answer last month may change after new data ingestion. Cognee's memory benchmarking work found that LLM-based scorers like DeepEval are prone to variance, which is why they rely on repeated runs and bootstrapped confidence intervals across evaluation cycles. Building reproducible memory states The hardest part of memory testing is not writing the tests. It is creating the conditions for tests to run reliably. Fixtures and seeding Create a canonical test dataset: a fixed set of documents, emails, and messages that represent known entities and relationships. Ingest this dataset before each test run to create a known starting state. The dataset should be small enough to ingest quickly but rich enough to cover your scenarios. Include edge cases: documents with conflicting information, overlapping entities, and time-sensitive data. Isolation Each test run must operate against an isolated memory state. Tests that share state interfere with each other, producing flaky results that erode trust in the suite. Pattern: create a dedicated test user per test suite, ingest fixtures for that user, run tests, then tear down the user's data after completion. In plain English: Think of it like setting up a clean database for each test run. Your memory system needs the same isolation guarantees you already expect from your application database tests. If two tests can see each other's data, your results are meaningless. Time simulation Freshness and sync correctness tests require time to pass. Waiting for real time is impractical in a CI pipeline. Mock timestamps and sync schedules so your tests can simulate "24 hours since last sync" without the wait. Evaluation beyond retrieval Retrieval accuracy is necessary but not the whole picture. The agent's final output depends on how the LLM uses the retrieved context, and that introduces its own failure modes. End-to-end evaluation A memory system that retrieves all the right documents can still produce wrong answers if the LLM misinterprets the context or ignores relevant information. LLM-as-judge evaluation is the emerging standard. Use a separate model to evaluate whether the agent's response is correct, complete, and faithful to the retrieved context. Hyperspell's Traces API records full agent interactions for later evaluation against these criteria. Human evaluation Sample-based manual review remains essential. Automated metrics correlate with quality but do not replace human judgment on subjective dimensions like helpfulness, tone, and contextual appropriateness. A practical approach: sample 5-10% of production queries weekly, have reviewers label relevance and correctness, and use the results to calibrate your automated metrics. A/B testing Compare memory system versions in production by routing a percentage of traffic to the new version and measuring downstream metrics: task completion rate, user satisfaction, follow-up query frequency. This produces the most reliable evaluation signal, but requires sufficient traffic and careful experimental design. Continuous testing in production Pre-deploy testing catches regressions. Production testing catches the problems that only appear at scale with real data. Canary queries. Run synthetic queries with known answers continuously against production. If a canary query starts returning wrong results, something in the memory system has changed. Anomaly detection. Track precision and recall over time. Set alerts for when retrieval metrics degrade beyond a threshold. Gradual degradation often signals data quality issues or sync failures rather than code bugs. User feedback loops. Thumbs up/down on agent responses is a noisy but valuable signal. Aggregate it over time to identify queries and topics where retrieval quality is consistently poor. For production monitoring patterns in depth, see our guide on memory observability. Building a memory testing practice Testing memory requires new patterns, not new tools. The shift from stateless to stateful changes what you test, how you build test data, and how you interpret results. A practical starting path: Start with retrieval evaluation. Build a ground truth dataset of 50-100 query-document pairs. Measure precision and recall. This gives you a baseline. Add regression tests. Pick your 20 most important queries and lock in expected results. Run them on every deploy. Build fixtures and isolation. Create a canonical test dataset and ensure each test run starts clean. Expand to integration tests and end-to-end evaluation. These require more infrastructure but catch problems the earlier stages miss. The field is early. Research confirms that evaluation protocols are fragmented and no standard has emerged. Teams that invest in test infrastructure now will compound their advantage as memory systems mature. Hyperspell's Evaluation API and trace recording are designed to make this testing loop accessible without building custom evaluation infrastructure from scratch. Frequently asked questions How do you test a non-deterministic memory system? Run multiple trials per test scenario and average results. Use bootstrapped confidence intervals to account for LLM variance. Focus on statistical properties like average precision and recall distribution, not exact-match expectations. What metrics should I use for retrieval evaluation? Start with Precision@k, Recall@k, and NDCG@k for ranked retrieval quality. Add F1-score for entity extraction accuracy. For end-to-end quality, use LLM-as-judge scoring. Together these cover both the retrieval and generation stages of a memory-backed agent. How do you build a ground truth dataset for memory testing? Three approaches: manually label which documents are relevant to each test query, review actual system outputs post-retrieval, or use LLM-based relevance scoring at scale. Synthetic generation (creating questions from known documents) is the most scalable method and requires no manual annotation. What is the difference between memory benchmarking and memory testing? Benchmarking measures system-level performance across standardized tasks (like MemoryAgentBench). Testing is what you build into your development workflow: unit tests, integration tests, regression suites, and evaluation pipelines that run on every deploy. Benchmarking tells you how your system compares. Testing tells you whether your latest change broke something. Key takeaways Traditional testing patterns break for memory systems because state is accumulated, not static. Same input, different output depending on context. Test five things: ingestion correctness, retrieval accuracy, permission enforcement, sync correctness, and freshness guarantees. Four test categories cover different failure modes: unit tests for deterministic components, integration tests for the full pipeline, retrieval evaluation against ground truth, and regression tests on every deploy. Reproducible testing requires fixtures, isolation, and time simulation. Without these, flaky tests erode trust in the suite. Handle non-determinism by running multiple trials and using confidence intervals, not exact-match expectations. Start with retrieval evaluation (50-100 ground truth pairs), then expand to regression tests, integration tests, and end-to-end evaluation.

title: How to Generate a Landing Page With AI
summary: AI landing page generation with Repaint. Use a prompt or existing content, add forms and calls to action, edit through chat, and publish free or on a custom domain.
body_text: Introduction Landing pages often need to be made quickly, but the traditional process still involves writing, design, and web development. New AI tools can turn a short description into a complete page in minutes, then let you revise it through chat. In this guide, I'll show you how to generate a landing page with Repaint . Why Generate a Landing Page With AI The main advantage is speed. Repaint can turn a short description into a complete first version in minutes. You can start reviewing the actual page without waiting for the copy, design, and development to happen separately. That speed makes it practical to give each campaign its own focused page instead of sending every visitor to a general homepage. The message and next step can match the ad or link that brought someone there. If the audience or offer changes, you can revise the page through chat or generate another version without starting a separate design project. Repaint can also use your existing website and brand assets as the starting point. New pages can match the rest of the brand without being built from a generic template. How It Works You begin by describing what you are promoting, who the landing page is for, and what visitors should do. An existing website or uploaded brand assets can also give Repaint content and design material to work with. Repaint uses those inputs to generate a complete first draft. After a few minutes, the page automatically opens in the editor. You can review the working page, make changes through chat, and add a built-in form or connect an outside service. The landing page can be published independently at a free Repaint address. Using an existing website as source material does not change or replace it. Once the page is ready, you can keep the Repaint address, connect a custom domain or subdomain, or add the page to a website that is already hosted in Repaint. Step 1: Describe the Page You start the process by describing the landing page you want in Repaint . The most useful description explains the offer, the intended audience, and the action someone should take after reading the page. A first message could be as simple as, "Create a landing page for a local painting company offering free estimates to homeowners in the Bay Area. Explain the service, include a few customer reviews, and collect project details through a form." That is enough for Repaint to begin planning the page. You can also mention where visitors will come from. Someone arriving from a search ad may need a more direct explanation than an existing customer following a link in an email. This context helps the page match the promise that brought the visitor there. The first prompt does not need to settle every detail. Repaint will give you a chance to clarify the direction before it generates the page, and anything can be changed afterward. Match Your Existing Brand If you already have a website, Repaint can use it as the starting point for the landing page. Share the URL, and Repaint imports the logo, colors, images, and business information it finds. This helps the new page match your existing brand without requiring you to recreate those details by hand. Repaint can also import public social profiles and uploaded files. You can add campaign images, product material, or a screenshot of a design you like. Repaint combines those sources with your instructions to create a page for the specific offer. Step 2: Generate a First Draft Once the direction is clear, Repaint starts generating the landing page. A typical page takes a few minutes. It writes the initial copy, incorporates the source material, and builds a responsive design for desktop and mobile. When the first version is ready, Repaint automatically opens it in the editor. The generated page is still a first draft. The offer may need a clearer explanation, the visual style may not fit the campaign, or the page may emphasize the wrong information. You can correct any of that through chat without generating the whole page again. Add Forms and Embeds A landing page usually exists to move visitors into another action. If you already use a booking calendar, registration form, or checkout tool, you can share its embed code in the Repaint chat. Repaint can place the service directly on the page so visitors can complete the next step without leaving it. An outside service can also stay on its own hosted page. In that case, Repaint can link the call-to-action buttons directly to that page. The landing page explains the offer, and the existing service handles what happens after someone clicks. For simpler lead capture, Repaint has its own form system. You can choose which fields to collect, where submissions should be emailed, and what visitors see after submitting. Those details can all be set up or changed through chat. Step 3: Edit With AI Most editing in Repaint happens through chat. You describe what you want to change, and Repaint updates the page and shows you the result. The same process can rewrite the copy, rearrange a section, or change the visual style. Text can also be edited directly on the page when you only need to make a small correction. If Repaint misunderstands a request, you can explain what was wrong and have it try again. Every update creates a new version, so you can restore an earlier one if an edit breaks something or you don't like the result. Generate Variants Once the first page is working, Repaint can use it as the starting point for variants. You can tell it what should stay consistent and what should change rather than building every page again from scratch. This makes it possible to reuse the design, brand assets, and form setup across a campaign. Repaint creates each variant as a separate page with its own URL. An advertising or testing platform can send traffic to those URLs and measure the results separately. Step 4: Publish Publishing puts the landing page online at a free address ending in sites.repaint.com. This is a public page that anyone with the link can visit. You do not need to enter a credit card or connect a domain before using it. The free Repaint address can be used for the campaign or as a staging address before connecting a custom URL. Because it is public, the page can also be shared with anyone who needs to review it. Publishing makes it possible to test the complete visitor experience. Form submissions should reach the correct inbox, and any linked or embedded service should work from the public page. Analytics and advertising scripts should also begin recording visits there. Making Changes After Publishing Publishing does not lock the page. You can keep editing while the current version remains online. The changes stay in a draft until you publish again, so a live campaign does not have to show work that is still being reviewed. When an update is ready, publishing again replaces the live page at the same URL. Existing campaign links continue working without any changes. Step 5: Choose a URL A landing page does not have to live on your main website domain. The right URL depends on how permanent the page is and how closely it needs to be connected to the rest of the website. The free Repaint address works for testing and can be enough for a temporary campaign. A landing page can also use its own custom domain or a subdomain such as offer.example.com while the main website stays with its current platform. If the main website is already in Repaint, the landing page can live on that site at its own path. If the main website is hosted somewhere else, it can simply link to the Repaint landing page. Pointing the main domain at Repaint only makes sense when you also want to build or migrate the rest of the website. Connect the Domain Through Chat To use a custom domain or subdomain, tell Repaint what you want to connect in the chat. It will provide the exact DNS records and explain where to add them based on the domain provider. The domain stays registered in the same account where it was purchased. Connecting a custom domain requires a paid plan. Current plans start at $20 per month when billed annually or $25 month to month, with full details on the pricing page . DNS changes often take effect within about 20 minutes, although they can occasionally take longer. Repaint secures the new address with HTTPS automatically. Once it is connected, open the final campaign URL and confirm that the page still loads and the next step still works. Conclusion AI is especially useful for landing pages because the work rarely ends with the first draft. Campaigns move quickly, and the page often needs to change with them. Repaint can generate the first version in minutes and handle later revisions through chat. That makes it much easier to create a focused page for each campaign instead of treating every one as another design project. You can generate a landing page with Repaint for free and decide whether the result meets your needs before paying. FAQ Do I need a website to create a landing page? No. Repaint can generate a landing page from a description of the campaign. You can publish it at a free Repaint address or connect a custom domain without having a separate website. Can I make the landing page match my existing website? Yes. Share the website URL, and Repaint can use its design and content as source material for the landing page. You can also upload additional brand files or campaign images. The existing website stays on its current platform while the new page is built and hosted separately in Repaint. Can I add my existing form or booking tool? Yes. If the service provides embed code, Repaint can place it directly on the landing page. It can also link a button to a form or booking page hosted elsewhere. For simple lead capture, Repaint has a built-in form system that emails each submission to you. Does a landing page have to be on my main website domain? No. It can use a free Repaint address, its own custom domain, or a subdomain connected to your main domain. If the main website is already in Repaint, the landing page can also live there at its own path. A website hosted somewhere else can simply link to the landing page. Can AI create landing page variants for A/B testing? Yes. Repaint can use one landing page as the starting point for variants and publish each one at a separate URL. Your advertising or testing platform can then split traffic between the URLs and measure which version performs better. Can I generate a landing page for free? Yes. Repaint lets you generate a landing page, edit it, add a form, and publish it on a Repaint subdomain without paying or entering a credit card. Paid plans start at $20 per month when billed annually or $25 month to month. They let you connect a custom domain, remove Repaint branding, and include more weekly AI usage. Full details are available on the pricing page .

title: Why Community Health Centers Matter to Millions of Americans
summary: Learn how community health centers expand access to care and why they play a vital role in supporting healthier communities.
body_text: National Health Center Week is an opportunity to recognize the community health centers (CHCs) that help millions of people access care each year. Their work supports healthier communities by connecting people to primary care, preventive services, maternal and child health support, behavioral health, social services and other resources that can shape long-term health. CHCs are community-based healthcare providers that offer primary care and other essential health services regardless of a person's ability to pay. They serve as a vital access point to care for nearly 52 million Americans, including many who may otherwise face barriers to healthcare. They play an especially important role for lower-income and medically complex populations, including more than 1 in 5 Medicaid beneficiaries . During National Health Center Week, Centene celebrates the important role these providers play in helping individuals and families access affordable, community-based care. In communities across the country, CHCs help expand access to care by providing primary care, preventive services, behavioral health services, maternal and child health support and chronic disease management close to where people live. Many also offer services such as translation assistance, patient education, care coordination and connections to community resources, helping patients overcome barriers that can make it harder to access care. "As a leading Medicaid managed care organization, Centene understands that CHCs are often where our members turn when they need care. For so many individuals and families, they're a trusted partner that knows the community, understands the challenges people face and provides them the care and support they need," said Alice Chen, Chief Health Officer, Centene. "At Centene, we know that improving health outcomes starts with meeting people where they are. CHCs are key partners for us in that work, from supporting healthy pregnancies and improving maternal health outcomes to managing chronic conditions like diabetes and high blood pressure and expanding access to behavioral health services. That's why we invest in CHCs: they help people get the right care at the right time and transform the health of the communities we serve." Alice Hm Chen, Chief Health Officer, Centene Centene is working with the National Association of Community Health Centers (NACHC) to support CHCs through partnership, tailored programs and a focus on value-based care and maternal and child health. Community Health Centers are Essential to Expanding Access CHCs play an important role in caring for Centene members, providing primary care to about 1 in 7 Centene members. Their presence in local communities helps connect patients to care close to home and supports access to services that address both medical and non-medical needs. Beyond clinical care, many CHCs help patients navigate barriers to health through services such as transportation assistance, translation support, patient education and connections to varied community resources. "What makes CHCs unique, and an essential part of the healthcare system, is that they are governed by patients for patients. Fifty-one percent of CHC board members are patients, and these patients receive the same wraparound care unique to their communities from their centers,” said Kyu Rhee, MD, MPP, CEO and President of NACHC. “At only 1% of the total U.S. healthcare spend, CHCs provide comprehensive whole-person care that extends beyond the exam room while operating on thin margins. Our partnership and Leadership Council with Centene seeks to address challenges CHCs experience in providing high-quality care to health center patients. CHCs need sustainable and diversified sources of funding and support in order to continue delivering services to 52 million patients, or 1 in 7 Americans, including 1 in 3 people in rural areas." Kyu Rhee, MD, MPP, CEO and President of NACHC How Centene Supports Community Health Centers Through Partnership Through its partnership with National Association of Community Health Centers (NACHC) , Centene supports CHCs by investing in provider collaboration, shared learning opportunities and programs focused on maternal and child health and value-based care. Value-based care emphasizes better health outcomes, preventive care and coordinated care while helping improve the overall patient experience. This work also includes local initiatives designed to strengthen how care is delivered. In Michigan, Meridian , a Centene health plan, embedded patient care advocates within four health centers across Southeast Michigan. These advocates worked directly with more than 12,000 Medicaid members, helping them connect with primary care providers, schedule appointments, navigate their care and stay up to date on preventive and social services. Centene Foundation has established a three-year, $3 million partnership with NACHC to support CHCs nationwide. In addition to the Foundation partnership, Centene and NACHC co-lead the Community Health Leadership Council, which brings together community health center leaders to share best practices and explore opportunities to strengthen care through areas such as value-based care and maternal and child health. Community Health Centers Support Maternal and Child Health CHCs are a critical source of maternal and child health services, providing prenatal, postpartum and pediatric care for families across communities nationwide. That role matters because maternal and child health depends on access to timely, coordinated care before, during and after pregnancy. CHCs are well positioned to support that care because they combine clinical services with community-based support. Through the Centene and NACHC partnership, participating health centers share ideas, learn from one another and identify practical approaches to improving care for mothers and babies through the Maternal Health Innovation Exchange. The partnership also supports programs focused on strengthening maternal care and improving health outcomes. These efforts build on the day-to-day role CHCs already play in helping mothers, babies and families stay connected to care. The partnership also supports broader efforts to strengthen CHCs nationwide. By investing in provider collaboration, maternal and child health initiatives and shared learning opportunities, the partnership aims to strengthen access to care and support healthier communities.

title: Terraform Your Fastly Config in a few Commands
summary: Import your complete Fastly setup into Terraform in minutes. No rewrites, no downtime, just your existing infrastructure, now as code.
body_text: Your Fastly infrastructure exists. You're managing services, security rules, TLS certificates, and logging endpoints every day. But when someone asks, "Is that in version control? Can we replicate it in another environment?"—the honest answer is probably no. Infrastructure as Code has become table stakes for serious DevOps teams. It's not optional anymore. Version control, auditability, disaster recovery, team collaboration aren't just nice-to-haves. But migrating an existing Fastly setup to Terraform typically means one of two things: abandon console management and rewrite everything from scratch, or manually map each resource to a Terraform definition. Both are painful and take weeks to implement. Luckily, there's a third way. Meet fastly-terraformer . The Problem We're Solving Fastly is powerful infrastructure. You've already invested time building your edge services, configuring backends, setting up Next-Gen WAF (NGWAF) security rules, and wiring logging. The problem isn't what you've built—it's that it's not in code. Terraform exists to solve this. But there's friction: you'd have to understand the full Fastly Terraform provider surface, manually inspect each resource in the console, and write import blocks for everything. For a complex setup that includes multiple services, dozens of domains, NGWAF workspaces with alert integrations the work can take a full weekend or even a week to complete. Or - in the worst case - it turns into something that never happens. Fastly-terraformer removes that friction entirely. How fastly-terraformer Works: One Tool, Just a few Commands The idea behind fastly-terraformer is simple. Point the tool at your Fastly account, and it discovers everything you've built, then generates the Terraform import blocks you need. No rewrites. No reinvention. Just your existing infrastructure, now code. Here's what it looks like: Copied! export FASTLY_API_KEY="your-fastly-api-token" export FASTLY_TF_DISPLAY_SENSITIVE_FIELDS="true" ./fastly-terraformer terraform init terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf terraform apply After those commands, your entire Fastly infrastructure is now under Terraform management safely, without changing anything running in production. Let's break down what happens under the hood: Step 1 : fastly-terraformer scans your Fastly account via the API and discovers all your resources—services, backends, domains, TLS certificates, NGWAF workspaces, key-value stores, everything. Step 2 : It generates an import.tf file containing Terraform import blocks for every resource: Copied! import { id = "abc123def456" to = fastly_service_vcl.my_service } import { id = "workspace-123/list-456" to = fastly_ngwaf_workspace_list.my_workspace_blocklist } Step 3 : You run terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf to fetch the actual resource configuration from Fastly, and Terraform writes it to generated.tf . You can learn more about how the -generate-config-out flag works in HashiCorp's Import Configuration Guide . Step 4 : terraform apply imports everything. Your infrastructure is now in state. Your Fastly config is unchanged. No downtime. No rewrites. You've just moved it from the console into version control. What Gets imported fastly-terraformer covers the full spectrum of Fastly infrastructure: Compute & Services : VCL services, Compute (WASM) applications, domains, backends, health checks, snippets, request settings, response objects. Security & WAF : NGWAF workspaces, workspace-scoped rules and lists, account-level security signals, alert integrations (Slack, PagerDuty, Datadog, Teams, Opsgenie, Jira, webhooks, mailing lists). Storage & Logging : Config stores, KV stores, secret stores, S3 logging, Syslog, Datadog, BigQuery, Splunk, and Papertrail endpoints. TLS & Access Control : TLS subscriptions, certificates, configurations, ACLs, and user management. That's 40+ resource types—essentially everything you can build in Fastly except legacy WAF (which has API limitations; use modern NGWAF instead). Two import modes give you flexibility: import your entire account at once, or scope to just NGWAF resources if you're moving security config to code first. The Benefits of Using fastly-terraformer Fastly-terraformer offers many benefits, such as: Speed. Teams spend weeks manually mapping Fastly resources to Terraform. fastly-terraformer does it in minutes. Team consistency. Once your infrastructure is in code, every team member sees the same source of truth. Changes go through pull requests, not the console. You get audit trails, peer review, and rollback capability. Disaster recovery. If something breaks, your infrastructure lives in a Git repo. You can redeploy from scratch with confidence. Environment parity. Need to spin up staging that matches production? Terraform + fastly-terraformer means you're not reverse-engineering from the console. Moat against vendor lock-in. Code is portable. If your team ever needs to migrate off Fastly, your infrastructure definition travels with you. Most importantly: your team stops maintaining infrastructure in two places (console + memory). One source of truth, one workflow, one set of standards. Getting Started Head to the fastly-terraformer GitHub repository . Installation guidance is in the README. Grab an API token from the Fastly console Set the environment variables Run the commands mentioned previously The tool handles the rest—including intelligent resource naming, conflict prevention for workspace-scoped resources, and graceful error handling if something fails mid-discovery. The Bottom Line Fastly is enterprise infrastructure. It deserves enterprise tooling. You wouldn't keep AWS or GCP infrastructure in the console—and you shouldn't keep Fastly there either. fastly-terraformer removes the last barrier to IaC adoption. Your Fastly setup can move to code today, not someday. No rewrites, no downtime, no weeks of manual work. Your config is already in Fastly. We just made it easy to version control. Ready to try it? Check out fastly-terraformer on GitHub . Have questions or want to contribute? Open a pull request to get started!

title: Cure Sanfilippo Foundation and National MPS Society Make $5.5 Million Strategic Investment in Spruce Biosciences
summary: Investment Broadens Patient Access to Tralesinidase Alfa Enzyme Replacement Therapy (TA-ERT) for Sanfilippo Syndrome Type B in the TA-ERT Expanded Access Program (EAP) TA-ERT EAP Expected to Initiate in the Fourth Quarter of 2026 SOUTH SAN FRANCISCO, Calif. --(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug.
body_text: Cure Sanfilippo Foundation and National MPS Society Make $5.5 Million Strategic Investment in Spruce Biosciences August 12, 2026 PDF Version Investment Broadens Patient Access to Tralesinidase Alfa Enzyme Replacement Therapy (TA-ERT) for Sanfilippo Syndrome Type B in the TA-ERT Expanded Access Program (EAP) TA-ERT EAP Expected to Initiate in the Fourth Quarter of 2026 SOUTH SAN FRANCISCO, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 12, 2026-- Spruce Biosciences, Inc. (Nasdaq: SPRB) a late-stage biopharmaceutical company focused on developing and commercializing novel therapies for neurological disorders with significant unmet medical need, today announced that Cure Sanfilippo Foundation and the National MPS Society have agreed to make a combined $5.5 million strategic investment in Spruce. The proceeds will be used to partially fund TA-ERT EAP, helping to broaden patient access to investigational TA-ERT for the treatment of Sanfilippo Syndrome Type B (mucopolysaccharidosis Type IIIB, or MPS IIIB). “We are deeply grateful to Cure Sanfilippo Foundation and the National MPS Society for their partnership and their conviction in Spruce’s development of TA-ERT,” said Samir Gharib, President and Chief Financial Officer of Spruce Biosciences. “This investment is a powerful expression of what we can accomplish when industry and the patient community work together. Their support helps us expand access to investigational TA-ERT for children with MPS IIIB who urgently need treatment options today, while we continue our work to bring this therapy to all eligible patients.” The strategic investment reflects a shared commitment among Spruce and two of the leading organizations serving the MPS and Sanfilippo communities to accelerate access to TA-ERT for the treatment of MPS IIIB, a devastating, rapidly progressing neurodegenerative disease that primarily affects children and for which there are no FDA-approved therapies. The Foundations’ and community fundraising efforts led to the initiation of EAP start-up activities earlier this year, including manufacturing of drug product, to accelerate access to children and families impacted by MPS IIIB in advance of potential U.S. FDA accelerated approval. “Every day without treatment matters for a child living with Sanfilippo syndrome. As both a physician and a parent in this community, I know the urgency families feel as they watch this devastating disease take abilities from their children,” said Cara O’Neill, M.D., Chief Science Officer and Co-Founder of Cure Sanfilippo Foundation. “The encouraging clinical data for TA-ERT offer meaningful hope, and our investment reflects the Foundation’s deep commitment to advancing rigorous science while bringing promising therapies within reach for children who need time-sensitive access. We are proud to stand alongside Spruce Biosciences, the National MPS Society and our community of families to support continued research and access to TA-ERT for the brave individuals facing this disease today.” Terri Klein, President and Chief Executive Officer, National MPS Society added, “For more than 50 years, the National MPS Society has worked to ensure that families affected by MPS are never alone in their fight, and that the research they place their hope in actually reaches them. Supporting Spruce’s Expanded Access Program is a meaningful step toward that goal for the MPS IIIB community. Investing directly in this effort reflects our belief that advocacy organizations can and should help bridge the gap between scientific progress and patient access. We are grateful to partner with Spruce and the Cure Sanfilippo Foundation to bring a potential treatment closer to the children and families who are counting on it.” TA-ERT Expanded Access Program The TA-ERT EAP is the planned open-label, single-arm early access program designed to provide TA-ERT to children in the United States with attenuated and severe MPS IIIB who are not eligible to enroll in the confirmatory study. To be eligible, a child must have a diagnosis of MPS IIIB confirmed by deficient N-Acetyl-Alpha-Glycosaminidase (NAGLU) enzyme activity and be between ≥12 and ≤60 months of age with a BSID-III-C raw score ≥70 or >60 months of age regardless of cognitive level. The program is expected to enroll approximately 10 participants across U.S. sites, with TA-ERT administered weekly via an intracerebroventricular (ICV) delivery device. Its primary objective is to allow early access to treatment with TA-ERT for those participants who are not eligible for inclusion in the confirmatory study while evaluating the safety and tolerability of TA-ERT. Participation in the TA-ERT EAP is anticipated to continue for up to approximately one year or until TA-ERT becomes commercially available, if approved. Spruce expects to initiate TA-ERT EAP as early as the fourth quarter of 2026. More information about the TA-ERT EAP can be found at ClinicalTrials.gov . About Sanfilippo Syndrome Type B (MPS IIIB) Sanfilippo Syndrome Type B (MPS IIIB) is an ultra-rare, serious, and fatal genetic disease characterized by deficiency in NAGLU, an enzyme required for the catabolism of heparan sulfate in lysosomes. It is estimated that MPS IIIB affects fewer than one in 200,000 people in the United States. The accumulation of toxic levels of cerebral spinal fluid heparan sulfate in the brain is the underlying pathophysiology of MPS IIIB. Although signs and symptoms of MPS IIIB can vary amongst affected individuals, progressive neurodegeneration typically follows a predictable path to brain atrophy, cognitive and developmental impairment, hyperactivity with aggressive and destructive behavior, delayed speech, hearing loss, and motor skill deficits. Somatic manifestations include coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, and gastrointestinal symptoms. The final stage of MPS IIIB is typically marked by severe dementia, loss of motor function, and seizure activity, with patients largely bed-ridden and requiring constant care, requiring feeding tubes for hydration and nutrition, and ultimately leading to death. The estimated life expectancy of individuals with MPS IIIB ranges from 15 to 19 years of age. Currently, there are no FDA-approved therapies for MPS IIIB, and management of the disease consists of limited palliative care to improve quality of life. About Tralesinidase Alfa Enzyme Replacement Therapy (TA-ERT) TA-ERT is a fusion protein comprised of recombinant human alpha-N-acetylglucosaminidase (rhNAGLU). TA-ERT is intended as an enzyme replacement therapy for the treatment of patients with MPS IIIB who lack rhNAGLU enzyme activity. TA-ERT is anticipated to restore rhNAGLU enzyme activity in the central nervous system following intracerebroventricular injection. rhNAGLU typically lacks the mannose-6 phosphate (M6P) residues that are essential for efficient cellular uptake via the M6P receptor pathway. As a result, the naked enzyme is poorly absorbed by cells, including neurons. To address this challenge, TA-ERT is fused to an insulin-like growth factor 2 peptide, which binds to the cation-independent M6P on cell surfaces. This fusion enables the enzyme to be internalized and delivered to the lysosome, thereby enhancing its therapeutic potential for treating MPS IIIB. By restoring NAGLU enzymatic activity and promoting clearance of lysosomal heparan sulfate and heparan sulfate non-reducing end in the brain, TA-ERT therapy is expected to preserve neuronal cell health and potentially halt or slow the neurological decline and improve clinical outcomes in affected patients. TA-ERT has been evaluated in three clinical studies in participants with MPS IIIB: the interventional study 201 and extension studies 202 and 401. TA-ERT has been administered to 22 individuals diagnosed with MPS IIIB, and has demonstrated an adequate safety profile based on integrated six years of safety data. About Spruce Biosciences Spruce Biosciences is a late-stage biopharmaceutical company focused on developing and commercializing novel therapies for neurological disorders with significant unmet medical need. Spruce’s lead product candidate, tralesinidase alfa enzyme replacement therapy (TA-ERT), is in late-stage development for the treatment of mucopolysaccharidoses type IIIB (MPS IIIB), or Sanfilippo Syndrome Type B, a devastating pediatric neurodegenerative disorder for which there are no FDA-approved therapies. TA-ERT has received Breakthrough Therapy Designation, Rare Pediatric Disease Designation, Fast Track Designation and Orphan Drug Designation from the FDA, as well as Orphan Drug Designation in the European Union. To learn more, visit www.sprucebio.com and follow us on X , LinkedIn , Facebook and YouTube . title: IHG expands voco hotels to Muar, Malaysia

This distinctive positioning makes voco hotels a strong fit for IHG’s first‑mover strategy in Malaysia, with the signing of voco Muar reinforcing the company’s ambition to enter high‑potential markets – building on its growing presence in destinations such as Kuching, Kota Kinabalu, Penang and Kuantan. Vivek Bhalla, Managing Director, South East Asia & Korea, IHG said : “The signing of voco Muar marks an important step in our strategy to expand into Malaysia’s high‑growth secondary and tertiary markets.
